title: AI as an Equaliser: How Technology Can Dismantle Barriers to Entry for Underrepresented Lawyers and Founders
bodyMarkdown:
*A Joint Whitepaper by Hemisphere Consultants and Knowledge Nexus*

---

**Executive Summary**

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping industries at unprecedented speed, creating efficiencies, unlocking new opportunities, and democratising knowledge. Yet its benefits are not distributed equally. For many women, minority professionals, and underrepresented founders, systemic barriers continue to restrict access to both AI tools and the ecosystems in which they thrive.

This whitepaper explores AI’s role as an equaliser in the legal and entrepreneurial arenas. It outlines how technology can help dismantle barriers to entry for underrepresented lawyers and founders, while also addressing the AI gender gap the structural imbalance that risks turning AI into another gatekeeper rather than a gateway.

---

**AI at a Crossroads**

AI is no longer on the horizon; it is here, embedded in daily workflows. From contract drafting to pitch deck development, its applications are vast. Yet, access remains stratified.

Lawyers from underrepresented groups often lack the networks, mentorship, and financial backing to compete with peers who benefit from established privilege.

Founders from diverse backgrounds face persistent challenges in accessing funding, markets, and visibility.

In two decades working across legal tech, strategy, and operations, Knowledge Nexus has seen first-hand that technology doesn’t transform industries, people do. And right now, the people driving AI adoption often reflect the same structural inequities that have long existed in law and entrepreneurship.

Lawyers from underrepresented groups still face barriers in accessing the networks, mentorship, and investment needed to meaningfully leverage these tools. Similarly, founders from diverse or non-traditional backgrounds continue to face disproportionate challenges in accessing funding, markets, and visibility. And at the level of the tools they build and deploy, studies of generative AI models show that women are under-represented in AI-generated imagery of professional roles, and algorithmic systems still embed gendered patterns (smiling women, male default for leadership roles).

If designed and deployed inclusively, AI has the power to change that. It can open doors, level access to knowledge, and amplify underrepresented voices, but only if we consciously build for it.

Recent research underscores both the pace and polarity of adoption. According to [LexisNexis](https://www.linkedin.com/company/lexisnexis/)’ AI Culture Clash report (Aug 2025), 61% of UK legal professionals now use generative AI for work, up from 46% just months earlier. The IDC and Relativity Generative AI in Legal study (Nov 2024) found that 48% of all AI use in legal is now generative, and 69% of professionals expect their usage to increase further within two years. Yet, only 17% of firms say AI is fully embedded in their strategy, suggesting enthusiasm without equal enablement.

The gap between experimentation and transformation is still a wide one. The challenge ahead isn’t just about deploying the next tool, it’s about ensuring that adoption is equitable, ethical, and effective.

If we look at the growing list of AI use cases in legal practice (see below) - these are only some of the main ones - it’s clear that this is an area that will only continue to expand in scale and sophistication.

Contract review & clause flagging Document review & due diligence eDiscovery & litigation support Legal research & summarisation Compliance & regulatory monitoring Legal operations & spend analytics Knowledge management & precedent retrieval Client-facing drafting support (pitch decks, proposals, client updates) Litigation analytics & case strategy Workflow & process automation

AI sits at a crossroads; it can either reinforce existing privilege and bias or it can redefine opportunity. The difference lies in how we lead, educate, and implement, and whether we make inclusivity part of the innovation process, not an afterthought.

[https://www.lexisnexis.co.uk/insights/the-ai-culture-clash](https://www.lexisnexis.co.uk/insights/the-ai-culture-clash) [https://resources.relativity.com](https://resources.relativity.com/)

---

**AI as an Equaliser**

**Levelling Knowledge Access**

Where once legal research or market intelligence required significant financial investment, AI-powered tools now deliver information at speed and scale. This enables underrepresented lawyers and founders to compete without prohibitive costs. Previously teams without deep networks and expensive subscriptions were forced to compete on less than equal footing. AI changes that dynamic.

These tools reduce cost and time barriers; tasks that once took hours (or days) can now be delivered in minutes. They open access to insights that were previously locked behind high cost or institutional ability. They bring scale to non-traditional practitioners: solo lawyers, diverse-founder start-ups, legal-ops teams outside major firms. They also hold enormous potential to improve access to justice. Take, for example, the opioid litigation cases in the US, where claimants were once buried under truckloads of discovery documents, tactics designed to exhaust smaller legal teams and inflate costs. Today, AI-powered review and eDiscovery tools could have surfaced critical evidence in hours, not months, dramatically reducing the resource gap between large corporate defendants and those seeking accountability.

---

**Automating Routine Work**

By automating administrative or repetitive tasks, AI frees up capacity for underrepresented professionals to focus on strategic growth, client relationships, and advocacy.

In every transformation project, from legal ops implementations to firm wide process reviews, one thing has always stood out: lawyers and legal professionals spend an extraordinary amount of time on low-value, manual work.

According to [Thomson Reuters](https://www.linkedin.com/company/thomson-reuters/) ’ *State of the Legal Market 2025* report, up to 40% of a lawyer’s time is consumed by routine administrative tasks such as document drafting, matter intake, and reporting. ([legal.thomsonreuters.com](http://legal.thomsonreuters.com/))

AI is rapidly shifting that balance. Automation tools can now generate first-draft contracts, summarise depositions, flag anomalies in discovery sets, and auto-populate matter trackers, saving both time and cost. A 2024 Law Society survey found that 63% of firms adopting AI reported measurable efficiency gains, and 52% said they had already redirected that time into higher-value strategic work. ([lawsociety.org.uk](http://lawsociety.org.uk/))

For underrepresented lawyers and smaller practices, this is not just about efficiency, it’s about equity. Automation narrows the operational gap between large firms with dedicated support teams and solo or small practitioners managing everything themselves. By shifting administrative burdens to technology, smaller players can compete on expertise and insight rather than scale of infrastructure.

---

**Expanding Mentorship & Networks**

AI can simulate aspects of mentorship, providing personalised guidance, curated learning paths, and even access to virtual communities. For those historically excluded from traditional networks, this represents a powerful levelling up mechanism.

**The AI Gender Gap**

Despite its promise, AI reflects the biases of those who build it. According to UNESCO, only 22% of AI professionals worldwide are women. This imbalance has real-world consequences:

Algorithms risk perpetuating existing discrimination.

Funding and hiring recommendations powered by biased data could systematically disadvantage women and minorities.

The absence of diverse perspectives in development stifles innovation and reinforces exclusion. Closing the AI gender gap is not just a moral imperative it is a business and societal one.

The [OpenAI](https://www.linkedin.com/company/openai/) 2025 usage report, however, signals a positive shift. The gender gap in AI adoption among users of ChatGPT has been narrowing rapidly. Women now represent a far greater proportion of professional users than in previous years, a trend attributed to growing awareness, better accessibility, and the integration of AI into mainstream professional workflows. ([cdn.openai.com](http://cdn.openai.com/)).

Yet, the structural barriers remain. Studies show that women are 63% less likely to secure venture funding for AI or tech driven startups compared to men ([oecd.org](http://oecd.org/)), and when they do, they often receive smaller investments despite equivalent performance indicators. In AI academia, women make up only 14% of authorship on leading machine learning papers ([next100years.org.uk](http://next100years.org.uk/)).

Beyond equity, the cost of imbalance is innovation itself. Closing the AI gender gap is therefore not only a moral imperative, but also a business and societal necessity.

Empowering more women to adopt, shape, and lead in AI will determine whether this technology becomes a force for fairness, or a mirror of our existing inequities.

---

**Pathways Forward**

For AI to serve as a true equaliser, action must be deliberate:

Inclusive Design: ensuring diversity is embedded in AI development, from datasets to decision-making frameworks. Accessible Training: Making AI literacy affordable and relevant for underrepresented lawyers and founders. Cross-Sector Collaboration: Leveraging the strengths of consultancies, law firms, tech hubs, and academia to create equitable adoption pathways. Ethical Governance: Advocating for policies that mandate transparency, fairness, and accountability in AI.

---

**A Shared Commitment**

[Hemisphere Consultants](https://www.linkedin.com/company/hemisphere-consultants/) and [Knowledge Nexus](https://www.linkedin.com/company/knowledge-nexus-ae/) share a commitment to creating pathways for underrepresented professionals.

**Hemisphere Consultants** breaks down barriers for underrepresented communities by taking a human first, community-centred approach that prioritises lived experience, authentic storytelling, and capacity building. They work directly with communities through listening sessions, partnerships, and representation-led strategies to ensure voices that are often excluded become central to decision-making and public narratives. Hemisphere champions these communities by bringing them into the design and conversation around AI, collaborating with organisations to reduce bias in their systems, and showing community members how AI can be used to amplify their own stories, businesses, and advocacy. In doing so, Hemisphere not only challenges systemic barriers but also equips communities to navigate and shape the technologies influencing their futures.

**Knowledge Nexus** contributes deep understanding of knowledge systems and technological integration, ensuring access is meaningful and sustainable. One is that they are particularly committed to the global student community. Through their free online community and training platform, future lawyers from any country can access practical resources on emerging topics like AI, digital transformation, and the future of law, helping them stay ahead of change, bridge skill gaps, and build globally relevant careers. The goal is to democratize access to knowledge and technology, empowering the next generation of legal professionals to participate fully in the transformation ahead.

Together, both organisations champion an inclusive AI future one that dismantles systemic barriers and enables diverse voices to thrive.

---

**Wrap up**

AI has the potential to be a leveller, dismantling barriers that have historically kept women and underrepresented groups at the margins of law and entrepreneurship. But this outcome is not guaranteed.

If inclusivity, accessibility, and ethical design remain central, AI can shift from a tool of privilege to a platform of possibility, empowering underrepresented lawyers and founders not just to participate, but to lead.

title: Leveraging AI in M&A: Lessons from GCs on the Frontlines
bodyMarkdown:
Most articles on AI in M&A read like they were written by a marketing team.

“AI will transform your legal department!”

But what does that actually mean for in-house lawyers, especially General Counsel leading M&A deals?

I had a conversation with [Bill Price](https://www.linkedin.com/in/bill-price/) a New York-based litigator turned GC who has spent the last two decades in the thick of M&A, from helping a SaaS firm IPO, to being the lead legal support for a $40 billion enterprise sales division at [AT&T](https://www.linkedin.com/company/att/) , to turning around and selling companies...

Let’s be honest, most of the content out there about AI and M&A is high-level fluff.

“AI will transform the deal process”… sure, but how?

And when it comes to AI and M&A, he’s got some *very real lessons* .

This isn’t theory. It’s lived experience.

#### 1. Being a tech GC instead of Being a GC in M&A.

The mantra? And one I'm putting in my back pocket for the future!

“Keep us out of jail and get things done.”

That’s it. That’s the role.

And it hit me, so many junior GCs get stuck in lawyer mode. They’re comfortable redlining contracts, negotiating clauses, fixing the messes. But what this GC kept saying is: *that’s table stakes* .

The real job is *driving the business forward* . He estimates his role is 95% business person, 5% legal operator.

**Here’s what that looks like in practice:**

Thinking strategically about the balance sheet.Anticipating problems before they blow up.Asking: how do we accelerate revenue, smooth bottlenecks, and position the company for a better exit?

That’s where AI starts to make sense, not as a shiny object, but as a tool to shift lawyers from reactive problem-solvers to proactive business leaders.

The real job is driving the business forward and growing the top line…

---

#### 2. Start Small, Prove Value

I know some of you are thinking: “But I don’t have budget for AI tools. The board isn’t going to approve some six-figure experiment.”

Good news: you don’t need it.

The smartest adoption I’ve seen is about picking *one small, high-impact problem* and solving it.

The GC gave this example: sales kept hitting the same contract red lines quarter after quarter. It was slowing revenue and frustrating everyone. By analyzing those patterns with AI, legal was able to rework the playbook, clear the bottleneck, and speed up deal closure.

That’s how you win buy-in. Start with the crawl stage. Solve something measurable. Prove value. Then expand.

---

#### 3. Crawl → Walk → Run in M&A

When you’re in the middle of a transaction, one of the first questions the GC asks the banker is: *“Which Virtual Data Room (VDR) are we using?”*

*Spoiler alert its not the only question you should be asking....*

That’s because due diligence lives and dies on how you manage documents.

This is where AI already shines:

Aggregating and structuring huge volumes of contracts.Summarising key clauses across multiple acquisitions.Flagging risk before it becomes a negotiation nightmare.

But don’t try to automate everything from day one. Crawl (targeted use cases). Walk (expand into playbook updates, dashboards, deal trackers). Then run (integrate AI across the full lifecycle of M&A).

---

#### 4. Optics and Influence Matter

One of my favourite stories from this GC was about optics.

They literally redesigned contracts to look better. Cleaner formatting, color logo, clearer visuals. Make the contract a differentiated product to sell.

Why? Because when a CEO or board member picks up a 60-page SPA, they don’t want to wade through walls of text. The legal substance didn’t change, but the perception of value did.

That’s the lesson for AI too. Don’t just *use* it, *communicate its value* . Show how it accelerates revenue. Show how it makes negotiations smoother. Show how it protects the business.

---

#### 5. Imposter Syndrome Is Real. But Flipping It Creates Influence

Many GCs feel like imposters when they first get pulled into board-level M&A discussions. You go from being the lawyer in the room to being expected to act like a business partner overnight.

Here’s the advice:

Embrace that shift. You *are* a business partner now.Let AI do some of the heavy lifting on the legal grunt work.Use the insights to drive higher-level conversations: *“Here’s where we keep losing time. Here’s the fix. Here’s the ROI.”*

That’s how you move from support function to strategic advisor.

---

#### 6. Don’t Chase Shiny Objects

Not all AI tools are worth it. This GC was clear: pick two or three with *real use cases* .

If e-discovery is your pain point, pick decoverAI; if it's M&A due diligence, pick Emma or from his experience with tech.

If your sales team is screaming about bottlenecks, start with analyzing approval authority processes and have AI build a streamlined playbook-publish it in Slack and build a culture of empowerment and autonomy

The trap is adopting tools because they look impressive, not because they solve your pain.

---

#### AI Won’t Replace GCs (except those who don't use it). It Will Make Them

It Will Make Them Indispensable

Here’s the truth: AI won’t make the GC redundant. It will make them more central and provide more time to be strategic to the business than ever before

But only if you approach it the right way:

Start small.Focus on business impact.Measure and communicate wins.Grow into bigger use cases.

M&A is one of the most complex, high-stakes things a GC will ever do. AI won’t take away that responsibility. But it can give you leverage, the kind of leverage that lets you move from being the lawyer cleaning up the mess… to the business leader who prevents it in the first place.

This is exactly why [Holly Cope](https://www.linkedin.com/in/holly-cope-ai-strategy/) & I are running a Global AI Skills Summit, it’s why we’re passionate about building community. It’s why our sessions will be about real stories by lawyers for lawyers. To help you walk away learning something that can actually be applied.

Our mission is simple: put people first.

We want every lawyer to feel empowered, not intimidated, by AI. We;re This community is here to help you: Understand the risks and rewards of AI in legal practice. Gain practical skills that you can use in your day-to-day work. Share experiences, challenges, and ideas with peers who are facing the same questions. Build confidence in using technology so you can thrive in a future where clients expect more. We know the legal world is full of noise, hype, fear, endless tools. This group cuts through that by focusing on what really matters: community, clarity, and capability.

[Give our page a follow to stay up to date on all things AI & Community](https://www.linkedin.com/company/the-global-ai-skills-community-for-lawyers/posts/)

[https://www.linkedin.com/company/the-global-ai-skills-community-for-lawyers/posts/?feedView=all](https://www.linkedin.com/company/the-global-ai-skills-community-for-lawyers/posts/)

title: Legal Tech Adoption: Why Culture Eats Strategy (and AI) for Breakfast
bodyMarkdown:
If you’ve followed me on here, you’ll know I spend most of my time talking about AI & tech in legal, the hype, the risks, the opportunities, and the lessons I’ve learnt over 20 years working with clients.

But here’s the part nobody likes to say out loud: **no technology works if nobody uses it.**

I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve sat with legal teams, both in-house and private practice, and heard some version of: *“Oh yeah, we’ve got loads of tools, or we’ve got X tool (I'm not going to name and shame the tool sorry guys* 👀)*… but no one actually uses it.”*

Lets take an in-house team I spoke to recently who invested in a workflow tool designed to give the GC oversight of team activity. Not to play “big brother,” but to generate insights they could share with stakeholders and the board.

On paper, it looked great. In reality? **Failure**

Why? Because the people and processes were left out of the buying decision.

The tool didn’t integrate with the systems lawyers actually use day-to-day: Outlook, Word, SharePoint. To the team, it was just another layer of admin… to *reduce admin.* You can guess the result: nobody used it, and the system that promised so much delivered nothing.

A strong Legal Ops team (or consultant) would have spotted this. This is part of the work I do daily, asking the questions lawyers don’t always think of, mapping the bottlenecks, and finding where real value comes from automating tasks. Notice what’s missing here: *tech.* Because the hard truth is, this was never a technology problem. It was a people and process problem.

👉 Lesson learned: **never buy tech until you truly understand how your people work.**

You can invest in the most advanced CLM, the slickest matter management system, or the smartest AI contract review tool. If lawyers aren’t logging in, if processes aren’t embedded, if the business doesn’t trust the outputs, you’ve just bought yourself very expensive shelfware.

And here’s the real kicker: **adoption isn’t about technology. It’s about people, trust, and culture.**

---

#### The Missing Piece: A Dedicated Legal Ops Role

In my last article, I talked about Legal Ops being the backbone of legal transformation. What I didn’t emphasise enough is this: you need someone with the time and capacity to make it all stick.

Too often, legal ops responsibilities are handed to already overstretched in-house lawyers “on the side of the desk.” The reality? Change initiatives stall, tools gather dust, and nobody owns the roadmap.

A dedicated Legal Ops role (or team) is not a “nice to have.” It’s the right hand of the CLO/GC. The function that:

**Aligns** the legal roadmap with wider business goals.**Translates** business priorities into legal initiatives.**Frees up** leadership to focus on lawyering and strategy.**Builds** the foundations for AI readiness and manages ongoing AI governance.

Think of Legal Ops as the strategic integrato**r** : making sure legal isn’t just supporting the business today but also anticipating where it’s heading tomorrow.

Without this, technology adoption is left to chance, and chance rarely delivers.

Lets put this into perspective. A GC once told me they wanted a contract tool. But here’s the thing, selling that internally as *“legal needs it”* or *“legal has a bottleneck”* rarely lands with a CEO or CFO. What lands with them are business challenges.

So I asked them: *why do you really need this?* And no, I didn’t want to hear about features or a tool that does x and y. I want to know what problem we are trying to solve.

Because here’s the truth no vendor is telling you...

Contract tech is usually the first thing in-house teams look at, but it’s also one of the vaguest. There are so many different angles:

Are you automating NDAs or simple contracts? Are you handling complex agreements? Or, like many businesses, are you actually dealing with mostly third-party paper, in which case, all that time spent automating your own templates - complete waste of time.

In this case, the business (a large global corporate) had a real issue: the materials needed to make their product didn’t arrive. Why? Because a supplier contract expired without anyone knowing. The contract had been managed by the business, not legal, and by the time legal were looped in it was already the eleventh hour.

Enter frantic negotiations. Because renewing a supplier agreement isn’t just about cost. It’s about:

**Compliance** with regulations, sanctions, and sector-specific requirements.**ESG obligations** , making sure the supplier still aligns with the company’s sustainability commitments.**What’s changed with the supplier** , financial health, ownership, operational capacity, or even geopolitical exposure.**Quality and delivery standards** , ensuring the goods meet the company’s requirements and timelines (missed deliveries can shut down production lines).**Pricing and indexation clauses** , particularly with inflation or currency fluctuations.**Termination and exit rights** , what happens if the supplier can’t perform or the company needs to pivot quickly.**Liability and indemnities** , especially around defective goods, IP, or product safety.**Data and confidentiality** , if the supplier touches sensitive information or has access to systems.**Risk allocation and insurance coverage** , to protect the business if things go wrong.

All of these are business-critical. Yet to the wider organisation, it often looks like legal is “delaying things” when in reality they’re protecting the company from supply chain disruption, reputational risk, and financial loss.”

But here’s the kicker: this wasn’t a problem that needed the shiny contract AI everyone is telling you about. It actually needed something far simpler, a robust contract management tool. One that allows business and legal to interact, that gives legal oversight, and that sets standards. Imagine a system that simply alerts you when a supplier contract is due to expire in 3–6 months. That alone would have avoided the crisis.

Now the GC has a story they can take to the CFO. Not “we need a tool because legal is drowning,” but: *“We need a tool to protect the company’s bottom line, to keep products moving, orders fulfilled, and revenue flowing.”*

And that’s the point: it’s no longer a legal problem. It’s a business problem. And that’s the language that gets buy-in.

---

#### Adoption Starts with People, Not Tech

Let me be blunt: the biggest barrier to adoption isn’t the tool. It’s the people.

Lawyers are trained to spot risks, not embrace change. That mindset means tech adoption will fail if it’s imposed rather than co-created. Legal Ops has to flip the script by focusing on three pillars:

#### 1. Culture & Trust

**Involvement builds trust.** If lawyers feel a system was “done to them” instead of “built with them,” adoption rates plummet.**Transparency matters.** Be honest about why changes are happening. Is it cost, efficiency, client service? The “why” is more important than the “what.”**Quick wins earn credibility.** Show people small, tangible benefits early, and you build momentum for bigger change.

#### 2. Training & Enablement

One lunch-and-learn won’t cut it. Adoption requires ongoing, bite-sized, embedded training.Different people learn differently, some prefer video demos, some written guides, some live sessions. Offering multiple formats is essential.Make training contextual. Show how a tool helps that lawyer in that workflow and real life scenario. They don't have time to try and figure this out themselves.

#### 3. Mindset & Change Management

Resistance often isn’t about the tool. It’s fear: fear of losing control, of looking slow, reputational risk if it goes wrong, of change itself.Change needs champions. Identify early adopters in the legal team, support them, and let them become your advocates.Communicate successes. Celebrate small wins, share metrics, and spotlight those who embrace the tools. Adoption spreads socially as much as it does procedurally.

---

#### The Role of Use Cases

Here’s another trap I see too often: buying tech because it looks shiny on a demo.

Without a clear **use case** , adoption stalls.

Legal Ops should always ask:

What problem are we solving?Who benefits most?How do we measure success?

Because when you roll out, that becomes your story.

It's not: “This AI tool can auto-redline clauses.” but “This reduces your review time by 30% so you can leave the office at 7pm instead of midnight.”

The best adoption journeys are rooted in pain points lawyers actually feel day-to-day. If it doesn’t make their lives easier, they won’t use it. Simple as that.

---

#### Continuous Improvement: Adoption Never Stops

Here’s the truth nobody tells you: adoption isn’t a project. It’s a long-term commitment.

Processes evolve as teams grow.Business priorities change.Tech vendors update features constantly.

If Legal Ops doesn’t keep iterating, measuring, tweaking, and adapting, adoption will slide. The best teams treat technology like a living process, not a one-off implementation.

I’ve seen plenty of tools launch with a grand launch, only to be quietly abandoned a year or two later. Why? Because nobody “owned” them. No one was responsible for updating workflows, retraining the team, or making sure the tool kept pace with other systems the business actually used.

Now compare that with the teams that build in regular “health checks”, every quarter they review how tools and processes are working, what’s changed in the business, and where the friction points are. Those teams don’t treat improvement as a one-off project; it’s just part of how they operate. And the result is obvious: adoption stays strong, value keeps building, and the tech doesn’t turn into yet another piece of shelfware.

---

#### Why All This Matters for AI

And here’s where this links back to AI.

AI isn’t plug-and-play. It requires:

**Trust in the outputs.** **Governance around use.** **Processes that can absorb change.** **People who are open to using it.**

Without adoption, AI in legal will never deliver on its promise.

Legal Ops is the glue: the team that sets foundations, builds trust, manages governance, and ensures that technology, whether CLM, analytics, or AI, doesn’t just get bought but actually gets used.

Get this right, and you don’t just roll out tools. You build a legal function that’s ready for the future.

title: Legal Ops Before AI: Why You Can’t Run Before You Can Walk
bodyMarkdown:
If you follow me here you'll know I talk a lot about AI in legal, the risk, the reward, the future. Many rambles of what I've learnt over 20 years advising and working with clients on all things tech.

But here’s the truth: without strong legal operations, AI will never deliver on its promise. It’s like trying to run before you can walk, or building a skyscraper without laying the foundations. Legal Ops isn't a cost centre, its the command centre and THE backbone to connecting legal with the wider business. Think a handshake that helps things run smoothly.

I once heard a client describe it perfectly, as the “below the table juggling balls.”

She said: imagine the balls above the table, the client discussions, the M&A deals, the litigation matters, and everything else in plain sight.

Legal ops is like the command room under the table, the part you don’t always see, but without it, the whole act falls apart. That’s where the broken links happen if it’s not running well.

Legal ops is that foundation. It’s the processes, systems, and culture that make technology work, whether that’s contract automation, AI-assisted review, or analytics dashboards. Without it, even the most advanced tools risk becoming expensive shelfware.

Many of my clients ask me to explain the what the why and the how so I hope this helps :)

#### What is Legal Operations?

Legal Operations, often called Legal Ops, is the business side of running a legal department or team. It involves managing people, processes, technology, and data to improve efficiency and reduce risk.

Think of Legal Ops as the engine room that helps lawyers focus on practicing law by handling the day-to-day operational details. It covers areas like budgeting, vendor management, technology adoption, and process improvement.

In today’s fast-paced legal environment, Legal Ops is key to transforming traditional legal teams into strategic business partners.

---

#### Why Legal Operations Matters

Legal departments face growing pressure to do more with less, delivering legal services faster, smarter, and more cost-effectively.

Legal Ops helps by:

Streamlining workflows and reducing repetitive tasksManaging and evaluating technology toolsEnhancing data-driven decision-makingImproving collaboration between legal and business teamsEnsuring compliance and risk management

Without Legal Ops, legal teams risk inefficiency, higher costs, and missed opportunities to add strategic value.

---

#### Key Roles and Responsibilities in Legal Ops

Legal Ops professionals act as a bridge between lawyers, IT, finance, and business stakeholders to keep the legal function running smoothly and aligned with company goals.

---

#### The Benefits of Legal Operations

By investing in Legal Operations, organisations can work more efficiently, control costs, strengthen risk management, and ensure compliance. All whilst freeing legal teams to focus on high-value work. It also opens the door to innovation, using technology and data more effectively. Legal ops is no longer a “nice to have”; it’s essential for any legal team that wants to thrive in today’s competitive landscape.

---

### Building your Legal Ops Function

#### Establishing a Legal Ops Team

Starting or refining a Legal Ops function begins with setting clear goals aligned to your organisation’s priorities, defining what success looks like, and securing leadership buy-in. From there, focus on assessing your legal team’s pain points, setting objectives like improving efficiency or managing costs, building a team with the right blend of operational, technical, and legal expertise, and creating strong communication channels between Legal Ops, lawyers, and the wider business.

It’s can also be worth bringing in external expertise where needed, someone who has seen both the wins and the failures with other clients, can ensure you’re building from the ground up in the right direction, and can act as a neutral intermediary when engaging with legal teams or the wider business to help sell the vision internally.

Remember culture over tech and trust wins adoption rates internally...

---

#### Defining Objectives and KPIs

Clear objectives guide Legal Ops efforts and make success measurable. Whether the aim is reducing contract turnaround times, cutting legal spend, or increasing technology adoption. Setting KPIs early, such as contracts processed per month, time to complete due diligence, percentage of spend under management, or user adoption rates for legal tech, creates accountability and helps justify ongoing investment.

One size rarely fits all. It’s imperative to understand your own processes, people, and workflows before you even start looking at tools, tech, or AI. Think of it like a plaster, do this the wrong way round and it won’t stick for long; do it the right way, and it sets you up for success.

---

#### Process Optimisation and Continuous Improvement

Legal ops isn’t about fixing something and moving on. I can see you all thinking of a tick box spreadsheet already and that magic complete button 👀

It’s a long-term commitment that works best when you’re willing to tweak and adapt. Often, you don’t truly know what a process needs until you start working with it. Mapping workflows helps spot bottlenecks and inefficiencies, and tools like process maps or case management systems can make tasks easier to visualise and streamline. The best results come from continuous improvement, regularly reviewing processes, gathering feedback, and adjusting tools and workflows as needs evolve. Teams and people change and processes and tech is no different!

---

### Using Case Mapping and Process Visualisation

#### What is Case Mapping?

Case mapping breaks complex legal matters into clear, manageable steps. From initial intake to final resolution, creating a detailed roadmap of the process.

In my experience, taking the time to map a case or transaction often reveals insights you wouldn’t spot otherwise. It helps teams clarify the scope of work, identify dependencies and bottlenecks, allocate resources effectively, improve coordination, and spot opportunities for automation or process improvement. By visualising the entire workflow, case mapping turns complex, often chaotic matters into structured, transparent plans that are much easier to manage and optimise.

Spoiler alert you can't do this without speaking to your people. You need to work with teams, find out who is involved in processes to map these out effectively. Yes I can hear you telling me that takes too long but trust me its worth the investment.

You're also setting up that all important TRUST element with your teams when you do roll any changes out as the right people would have been involved so it works. I'm not saying involve every member of every team, thats not logical but the rest of the team will feel heard if the right one was involved.

---

#### Identifying Bottlenecks and Opportunities

Clear, visual overviews of every step in a legal process, makes it easier to see where delays or inefficiencies occur.

In my experience, they often highlight things like redundant approvals, repetitive manual data entry (I see you teams with 4 systems that you enter the same information into 👀), or bottlenecks from unclear handoffs.

Once these areas are identified, Legal Ops can take targeted action, redesign workflows, reallocate resources, or introduce automation to handle repetitive tasks. Tackling these pain points proactively helps streamline processes, cut turnaround times, and improve the overall quality of legal work. Remember its not always about working faster, but working better.

---

#### Real-Life Examples

I'm going to give you a lifeline here. 20 years of working with lawyers has shown me the use case list is endless, across every function but here are some examples to set the scene better.

**Reducing Contract Review Times**

A client faced delays in their contract review process due to unclear workflows and multiple handoffs between legal, procurement, and business teams. By mapping out the entire contract lifecycle, from request to final signature, they identified redundant review steps and bottlenecks caused by inconsistent approval protocols.

We redesigned the workflow to streamline approvals and introduced automated reminders for pending tasks. As a result, the contract review cycle time was reduced, enabling faster deal closures and improved stakeholder satisfaction.

Note how I didn't even mention AI here 👀

Its not always AI thats needed sometimes it's just straight forward automation. We're quick to want those shiny new things without really thinking is it for me. Don't get me wrong I had a similar client to the above where they also were wasting time on trying to match previous precedents during the review phase. This is where AI comes in and can help with the redlining phase. I also had another where the M&A team simply needed to review risky clauses quickly. Enter the tool which allowed us to pre define those clauses and then analyse 20,000 contracts (yes imagine going through those manually...) extracting said clauses and providing a nice XLS report for the lawyers to do the lawyering. I mean as nice as an XLS report can ever be...

---

### Technology in Legal Operations

Now lets get into what you know is my favourite subject. Legal Tech. I talk a lot about not running before you can walk which I stand by but tech is also the magic that glues all that prep work together.

---

#### Legal Tech Categories

Legal tech covers a broad range of tools designed to improve different parts of legal work. Understanding these categories helps you focus on solutions that truly meet your team’s needs. Remember rarely does one size fits all work. It has to fit THE use case and THE people. An example of some different types for you:

**Matter Management:** Software that centralises all case-related information, documents, deadlines, and communications. It helps legal teams organise workloads, track progress, and improve collaboration across departments.**Contract Lifecycle Management (CLM):** Tools that automate and streamline the entire contract process, from drafting and negotiation to approval, storage, and renewal reminders. CLMs reduce errors, speed up cycle times, and improve compliance. These have had a face lift since the boom of AI as now many can do this and more. AI brings in things like being able to auto redline and speed up review parsing a clause in a new contract to those in your fallback positions. **E-discovery and Document Review:** Platforms that support efficient collection, processing, and review of large volumes of documents for litigation or investigations. Many include features like AI-assisted tagging, deduplication, and predictive coding to reduce manual review effort.**AI-Powered Assistants and Analytics:** Advanced AI tools that can answer questions about documents, summarise content, flag risks, and provide insights based on legal data. They help teams make faster, more informed decisions and identify hidden risks early.**Legal Research Tools:** Databases and AI-enhanced platforms that help lawyers quickly find relevant cases, statutes, and legal precedents, saving hours of manual research.**Compliance and Risk Management Software:** Tools that monitor regulatory changes, automate compliance workflows, and help manage risk across jurisdictions.**Billing and Time Tracking:** Applications that simplify tracking legal time and expenses, automate billing processes, and integrate with finance systems for improved accuracy.**Collaboration Platforms:** Secure communication and document-sharing tools designed for legal teams and external counsel to work together seamlessly and maintain confidentiality.

---

#### Evaluating Tech

When choosing technology, it’s important to think beyond the shiny demo features. Ask yourself: does it solve your specific pain points? Is it intuitive for your team to use? Can it integrate with existing systems? Does it meet legal and data privacy requirements? And finally, what level of vendor support and roadmap can you rely on?

That's all for now, next up will be around driving technology adoption and change management. After all no tech works if no one adopts it.....

Let me know if this was useful and what else you'd like to know?

#LegalTech #LegalOps #Innovation #Legal #KnowledgeNexus #EducatingLawyers #LegalEducation #AI #FutureOfLaw

title: eDiscovery Reimagined: From Regex to Real‑Time AI Agents
bodyMarkdown:
For decades, legal teams wrestling with mountains of documents and messages developed advanced regex queries, sometimes called needing a “Relativity degree” to manage discovery. But today, AI is transforming eDiscovery, making your team faster, smarter, and less reliant on manual searching. Tomorrow I'll be co-hosting an event to talk around exactly this with [TransPerfect Legal](https://www.linkedin.com/company/transperfect-legal/) [Ladies In LegalTech - UAE](https://www.linkedin.com/company/ladiesinlegaltechuae/) [Women in eDiscovery™](https://www.linkedin.com/company/women-in-ediscovery/) [Knowledge Nexus](https://www.linkedin.com/company/knowledge-nexus-ae/) at [DIFC Academy](https://www.linkedin.com/company/difcacademy/).

**Why the old way is breaking down**

Complex Regex = Hidden Risk: Court mandates, Slack channels, PDFs, images, audio. Regex search can't keep pace.Week-long reviews = high cost and mental fatigue.Gatekeepers become data bottlenecks.

**Enter AI‑Powered eDiscovery** 💡 Instead of crafting lines of code, modern tools use **TAR** , **entity recognition** , **thread reconstruction** , and **audio transcription** to automatically surface relevant content and thread conversations together.

**Key Benefits**

**Speed** : First-pass review in hours, not days.**Breadth** : All data types included: chat, voice, video.**Context** : AI groups conversations, highlights stakeholders, surfaces sentiment and anomalies.**Efficiency** : Costs drop, relevance rises; key docs found without human guesswork.

**Mitigating Hallucinations & Overreach**

Generative AI can mislabel or hallucinate context, but top platforms build in **human-in-the-loop validation** , **confidence scoring** , and **continuous retraining** .

**Impact in Practice**

Consider a Dubai litigation team faced with a month’s worth of encrypted WhatsApp threads and voicemail recordings. Using AI agents, they processed it within hours. Transcribed, tagged speakers, and surfaced key decision points. Outcome? Crucial documents were uncovered before the deadline, saving weeks of review and tens of thousands of dirhams. Now they aren't just accepting the output but it does mean key risks can be flagged much quicker for that intense human review and strategy decision making...

**Takeaway for Clients & Lawyers**

eDiscovery isn't just about finding documents, it’s about telling the story behind them. AI helps you map timelines, track communications, and present coherent narratives. And you don’t need coding credentials, just a partnership between AI tools and human judgment.

Wave goodbye to regex and say hello to intelligent review. By blending technology and legal insight, firms can deliver faster, more accurate discovery and higher-value counsel.
